title: Besides increase in business revenue, what are notable films that have made a long-standing societal impact?

commenti.body: Not exactly the most positive example but Birth of a Nation immediately revived the Ku Klux Klan and created and reinforced a lot of racial stereotypes against African Americans that still exist today.

The run of “scientists aren’t nerds they’re cool” movies is interesting to look back on.  

Let’s say it started with Jurassic Park and  ran thru Twister and Dante’s Peak.  Many kids watched those and said, “I want to go to grad school and save the world!”.  

Those kids got wrecked with student loans, 2008 financial crisis, no job prospects.  The first election they voted in or paid attention to was invalidated by the Supreme Court. (Bush v. Gore).  And the world keeps getting hotter, just like Gore said it would.

Yeah, Triumph of the Will was the other one that came to mind unfortunately. 

I would say also arguably that 50s sci fi movies in general gave birth to a lot of the UFO culture that still exists today. Same thing with stuff like JFK that fed into a burgeoning conspiracy theory culture. 

You could probably also cite a lot of documentary movies. Certainly Michael Moore’s movies had some political effect, for example. 

Subculture movies in general … from Beatnik films to surf movies to punk rock to hip hop, movies have picked up on and magnified existing subcultures making them more mainstream.

A little bit tangential but, in your mind, would this be a case of art causing violence? Outside of "Birth of a Nation" I think there's a fine or arguably non existent line between art versus propaganda (used in a denotative way) where context/motive begins to blur output. So would the logic then be that films like this can be said to cause violence directly due to it being a propaganda piece or is it a tenuous differentiation given the artform it takes? Birth of a Nation is definitely one the "better" examples.

Rocky Horror Picture Show birthed the idea of the “cult film” and even now (almost 50 years after its initial release) you could likely find a midnight showing in almost any city, big or small, anywhere in America.

It would be interesting to see the increased depiction of college students in films compared to the national rate of new applicants. Before, college used to be known for the elite, managerial class who would often inherit family run businesses or seek specializations. Because of the greater ease of access to (community) colleges and universities, there's likely been some upward but contrasting trend of young adults in movies. This was most apparent in teen comedy/college party movies which further normalized college to the youths.

I think there has always been a natural interest by youth for higher education due to its once exclusivity. While yours focuses more on the science role, the college point in general would be the most interesting to see in film over the years.

*The Matrix* has had a few big cultural effects: 

It’s not controversial at all to say that it pushed us into two major technological transitions (which each ushered in various cultural and economic/industry changes). First, it was what made DVD players and DVDs finally start taking off. Instead of having a dozen or so VHS tapes, it became common for people to start having much larger collections of movies—and even TV shows!—available to watch at home, on demand.

Then, ten years later, when Netflix was trying to create a market for streaming professionally produced content over the internet, they did so by…putting *The Matrix* front and center in their advertising images for their new streaming benefit that DVD subscribers got.

Entire books can and have been written about the cultural impact of each of those new technologies. They existed before *The Matrix*, but in each case, *The Matrix* was the marketing tool that took the technology mainstream.

More controversially, *The Matrix* has had a very clear legacy in American politics—one which the writers/directors lament. The various cultural threads that we now know as “the red pill movement” would have existed without *The Matrix*, but the movie gave them a central metaphor to make some of their arguments and provide their people with a durable group identity. Who knows what that movement would have looked like without *The Matrix* being as ubiquitous in American culture as it has been.

> Subculture movies

These definitely crossed my mind but those films exist as a result of an outside movement and not the other way around. If, for example, a given subculture rose as a direct result of a film or film movement then fair enough. My motive is more about examples of a film that has been used for vehicles of change. While a film that helps popularize groups of people or ideas counts, I'd argue the originator of that change isn't the film but the actual group or people ideas in the first place.

Yes for sure but it’s all about the zeitgeist with these things, very few films emerge in a vacuum and then cause massive change as a result. But a lot of them cause things much bigger than they originally were. I was going to cite Rocky Horror because that is a film that has lived for 50 years and still engenders community cult showings. But it’s not really a social movement in the way you phrased your original post.
I guess you could also argue things like John Waters movies in general having an extremely outsized influence on LGBT culture in the US. Maybe even Kenneth Anger.

I think, one more, is that it was one of the earlier films that introduced Japanese elements -- specifically Ghost in the Shell -- to a mainstream Western audience. While anime found representation in early hyper-violent DTV OVAs, graphic novels, and video games, it is The Matrix that truly first coupled the mainstream with the narrow geek culture after the success of Star Wars. Hence, while the inspirations of the Matrix can be said to be a pastiche of personal and borrowed aesthetics of other subcultures, the film really set the tone for, better and worse, current day Hollywood's adoption of Japanese pop culture.
